name: Quincy Treadwell
languages: Spanish, from a grammar, badly but improving every day south of San Antonio
equipment: A borrowed black frock coat, too short in the sleeves, which belonged to the judge
Derringer (Remington over-and-under), 2 rounds loaded, given him by Mrs. Dunagan from the judge's desk, which he has fired once, at a fence post, and missed
Boot knife, which he uses to sharpen pencils
Notebook and pencil (four notebooks, filling fast)
A copy of the Revised Statutes of Texas, a copy of the federal Enforcement Act of 1870 cut from a newspaper, and the judge's own commonplace book
The key to Judge Brisco's chambers in the Lockett County courthouse
A chessboard that folds into a box, and a deck of playing cards he is learning to read faces over
Saddle and tack, bedroll, canteen, a straw hat that does not suit him
Riding horse: the judge's old sorrel mare, Portia, who knows more about Texas than he does
features: Book Learning (Back East origin: advantage on Investigation checks to read documents, deeds, tax rolls, ledgers and forgeries; once per long rest he recalls one useful fact of law, procedure or history without a check; lawyers, judges and editors treat him as one of their own; disadvantage on his first Riding or Survival check in front of strangers each day, which the vaqueros find very funny)

Read the Table (Gambler: proficiency doubled for Gambling and Insight checks; once per short or long rest, after a minute watching or questioning someone, he learns one thing they are hiding; he reads a witness the way the judge taught him)

Ace in the Hole (Gambler: once per turn, an extra 2d6 damage with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm when he has advantage, an ally is next to the target, or the target believed a bluff in the last minute; not part of the damage on his sheet)
Lady Luck (Gambler, 2nd level: 2 luck points per long rest, each spent to roll an extra d20 and choose, or to make an attacker reroll)
Sleeve Gun (Gambler, 2nd level: he draws a concealable weapon as a bonus action unnoticed and can Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action)

Game: Riverboat Charmer (Gambler, 3rd level: a person he has talked with for an hour treats him as a friend until given reason not to, and will do him a favor that costs nothing without a check; it is how he gets into courthouses, records rooms and sheriffs' offices)
Ability Score Improvement (Gambler, 4th level: +1 Wisdom, +1 Charisma)
The Schoolhouse (Schoolteacher background: he taught at the Jubilee school for two years before reading law; Jubilee's families trust him and their children tell him everything)

personality.traits: I talk fast when I'm frightened and faster when I'm right. I cite statutes at dinner. I write everything down. I am painfully polite, and I lose every argument about horses.
personality.ideals: The law is the only thing that stands between a man like Lucius Vandiver and a man like Isom Haywood. It stood there very badly this spring. That is a reason to make it stand better, not to give up on it.
personality.bonds: Judge Nathaniel Brisco, who took in an Ohio schoolteacher with no money and taught him the law, and who died with my name on a letter in his desk. The children of Jubilee, whom I taught to read. Abner Ruthven, whom I have never met and have written to four times.
personality.flaws: I am a coward with a gun, a fool on a horse and an innocent about men like Gattis. I also have a secret: I was in the judge's study until nine on the night he died, and I saw Spratt's boy watching the house from across the street, and I went home and did not tell anyone, because I was afraid. I have not forgiven myself.

appearance: A tall, thin, stooped young man of twenty-four with a long earnest face, wire spectacles, a cowlick, ink on his fingers and a borrowed black coat too short in the sleeves. He rides badly and sits a chair at a records room counter as if he were born there.
backstory: Quincy Treadwell was born on a farm near Elyria, Ohio, in 1850, went to Oberlin College on a scholarship, and came to Texas in 1871 with the American Missionary Association to teach freedmen's children, which is how he came to teach at the Jubilee school for two years under Reverend Solomon Burris. Judge Nathaniel Brisco saw him arguing with a cotton buyer over a Jubilee family's weights in 1873, liked him, and took him on as a law clerk. He was at the judge's side all winter, copying the deeds and the statements that went into the packet, and he wrote the press copy of the judge's letter to Abner Ruthven in his own hand. He left the judge's house at nine on the night of 5 April; he heard the shots from his boarding house. Since then he has sat on the courthouse steps every evening watching bounty hunters go up to the Stock Association office, trying to find one worth talking to. On Wednesday 15 April, he finds the party.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Quincy is the party's way into the case in lb-scenario-001: he finds them on Wednesday night and tells them to look at the window, the ball and the deed book. He has the judge's chambers key, knows about Ruthven and the grand jury (CLUE D2), and taught at Jubilee, so Mother Lytle will talk to anyone he brings. He becomes a companion if the party ask him to ride with them, and is useful all the way south: he reads every document at advantage, knows the law on both sheriffs' claims at Crow's Ford, can tell Fenner what immunity Ruthven might offer, and is the one person who can explain to Isom, in the judge's own words, what testifying would mean. He is terrible at everything physical; let the vaqueros and Wiley teach him, and let him get better, slowly.
dmNotes.voice: Fast, precise, earnest, with sudden Latin and long subordinate clauses, and an Ohio flatness. Says 'with respect' before disagreeing with anyone, including people pointing guns at him.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: the packet in Ruthven's hands by 1 June. Secondary: Isom alive. Tertiary: to be the kind of lawyer the judge was.
dmNotes.secrets: He saw Spratt's boy watching the judge's house at nine o'clock on 5 April and told no one. Confessing it to the party (when he trusts them, or when someone asks why he looks sick at the word 'Spratt') is evidence that the murder was planned and watched, and it is the moment he stops being a boy. He also wrote the press copy of the letter that Spratt read; he blames himself for the judge's death, unfairly.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: hopeful, then devoted. Toward Reverend Burris: a son's respect. Toward Ulysses Wardlow: awe at a federal officer who has read the statute. Toward Valentine Shreve: fascinated disapproval; they play cards every night and Quincy loses every hand until the night he doesn't. Toward Vandiver and Spratt: a cold, articulate hatred he did not know he had.
